blog.planA.declared: Declared chips. Counted under the deal, in buildings inspectors can visit.
blog.planA.uncounted: Capability gains from improved methods and software using existing chips.
blog.planA.figureDescription: The diagram starts with 220 declared chips inside a boundary. As the essay progresses, 320 marks appear outside it, representing capability gains from software and methods using existing hardware. The illustration asks whether a chip count is enough to track those gains; the marks are illustrative, not measured quantities.
blog.openjev.caption.0: The first run scored 0.704 on the confirmatory split's 2015 tests.
blog.openjev.caption.1: The same weights scored 0.637 on holdout and 0.624 on exploratory.
blog.openjev.caption.2: All three archive splits cover nearly the same dates.
blog.openjev.caption.3: The overlap and label-noise checks didn't explain the accuracy gap.
blog.openjev.caption.4: Switching to Bradley-Terry raised accuracy from 0.637 to 0.775.
blog.openjev.caption.5: VERA avoided the worst variant in 90.3% of Upworthy tests.
blog.openjev.caption.6: These results use Upworthy headlines from 2013–2015. Email performance is untested.

blog.planA.caption.2: Improved methods can increase capability without adding chips.
blog.planA.caption.3: The chips are still counted, but what runs on them is unknown.
blog.planA.caption.4: Work can remain unpublished while research is ongoing.
blog.planA.caption.5: Inspecting declared chips does not establish everything the software can do.
blog.planA.caption.7: The same chips, spread out and shared.
blog.planA.caption.8: The uncounted part starts to organise itself.
blog.planA.caption.9: A fixed chip count does not necessarily imply a fixed level of capability.
